text:
Multi-year simulations
If the user does not enter specific modifications, successive years repeat the same monthly pattern of climate and demands.
This makes it possible to study the cumulative effect of repeated seasonal conditions, but does not represent a historical or future series with interannual variability.

title: Assumptions, limitations and appropriate use
Assumptions, limitations and appropriate use
text:
Calibration
The hydrological and groundwater-interaction parameters were fitted using monthly data from six gauging stations on unregulated river reaches.






Important



The results should be interpreted as the model’s response to assumptions defined by the user, not as a certain prediction of the basin’s future behaviour.

title: H2OSEG-Ter
text:
H2OSEG-Ter is a web tool for exploring how changes in climate, land use and water management may affect flows in the Ter river, the volume stored in reservoirs, compliance with environmental flow requirements and the extent to which water demands are met.
The tool runs directly in the browser and requires neither installation nor registration.
Open H2OSEG-Ter

title: H2OSEG-Ter
section: What can it be used for?
text:
What can it be used for?
H2OSEG-Ter is designed to:

Quickly compare alternative scenarios.
Explore the effects of changes in precipitation or temperature.
Modify urban and agricultural water demands.
Modify specific abstractions or reservoir releases.
View simulated flows throughout the river network.
Identify reaches that fail to meet environmental flow requirements.
Detect demands that cannot be met.
Observe changes in reservoir storage.







Important



H2OSEG-Ter is a tool for exploring and comparing scenarios. It is not a hydrological forecasting system or an operational model for making legal or real-time management decisions.

title: Drainage-area contributions
Drainage-area contributions
Drainage-area contributions
text:
Evapotranspiration
Monthly potential evapotranspiration is calculated from mean monthly temperature using the Thornthwaite method:
\[
PET_m =
16
\left(
\frac{10T_m}{I}
\right)^a
K_m
\]
where:
\[
I=\sum_{m=1}^{12}
\left(
\frac{T_m}{5}
\right)^{1.514}
\]
and:
\[
a =
6.75\times10^{-7}I^3
-
7.71\times10^{-5}I^2
+
1.792\times10^{-2}I
+
0.49239
\]
\(K_m\) corrects the result for day length and the number of days in the month.






NoteInterpretation





PET represents the evaporative demand of the atmosphere if sufficient water were available. It is not necessarily the amount of water actually evapotranspired by the basin.



For each land use \(u\), actual evapotranspiration is calculated using a formulation based on precipitation, PET and a vegetation coefficient1:
\[
ET_{i,m}
=
\sum_u f_{i,u}
\,
P_{i,m}
\,
\frac{
1+w_u\frac{PET_{i,m}}{P_{i,m}}
}{
1+w_u\frac{PET_{i,m}}{P_{i,m}}
+\frac{P_{i,m}}{PET_{i,m}}
}
\]
where:

\(f_{i,u}\): proportion of land use \(u\) within area \(i\);
\(w_u\): evapotranspiration coefficient for the land use;
\(P_{i,m}\): monthly precipitation;
\(PET_{i,m}\): potential evapotranspiration.


Coefficients by land use



Land use
\(w_u\)




Water
0

0

1.75

Higher values represent a greater capacity of vegetation to use the available water.






Warning



The model represents the effect of land use on evapotranspiration in an aggregated manner. It does not explicitly simulate soil moisture, rooting or vegetation growth.

title: Model overview
text:
The model represents the river basin as a directed graph:

nodes are points where flow is generated, modified, stored, diverted or assessed;
edges are river reaches that carry water downstream.

This structure makes it possible to explicitly follow the path of water from the headwaters to the lower reaches of the basin.

text:
The model represents the river basin as a directed graph:

nodes are points where flow is generated, modified, stored, diverted or assessed;
edges are river reaches that carry water downstream.

This structure makes it possible to explicitly follow the path of water from the headwaters to the lower reaches of the basin.

title: Model overview
Model overview
text:
Calculation sequence
For each node (i) and month (m), the general balance can be expressed as:
\[
Q^{out}_{i,m}
=
\max\left(
0,\,
Q^{in}_{i,m}+\Delta Q_{i,m}
\right)
\]
where:

\(Q^{in}_{i,m}\) is the sum of flows arriving from upstream;
\(\Delta Q_{i,m}\) is the local change in flow;
\(Q^{out}_{i,m}\) is the flow leaving the node.

Local changes can be:

positive: contribution from a drainage area, return from a treatment plant or external inflow;
negative: urban, agricultural or other abstraction.

Flow cannot become negative. When demand exceeds the available water, the difference is recorded as unmet demand and downstream flow is set to zero, assuming that all available water is abstracted to meet the demand.

title: Model overview
Model overview
text:
Browser implementation
Calculations are performed in the user’s browser. The computational graph and simulation variables are updated after each scenario change, and the results are displayed on the map and in information tables.

title: Creating and comparing scenarios
text:
A scenario is a modification of the reference conditions. It does not necessarily represent a prediction, but rather a question such as:

What would happen to river flows if precipitation decreased, demand increased or reservoir releases changed?

title: Creating and comparing scenarios
Creating and comparing scenarios
text:
Modifying precipitation
A 20% reduction means that, for each affected month:
\[
P'_{i,m}=P_{i,m}(1-0.20)
\]
where (P_{i,m}) is the reference precipitation and (P’_{i,m}) is the modified precipitation.

title: Creating and comparing scenarios
text:
Modifying temperature
An increase of 2 °C is applied as follows:
\[
T'_{i,m}=T_{i,m}+2
\]
The change affects potential evapotranspiration and, indirectly, actual evapotranspiration and river contributions.

title: Creating and comparing scenarios
text:
Modifying demands
Demand scenarios multiply the abstractions associated with each category. For example, a 10% increase in agricultural demand means:
\[
D'_{m}=D_m(1+0.10)
\]

title: Creating and comparing scenarios
text:
Modifying forest cover
This scenario modifies the proportion of forest in each drainage area relative to the reference value. When forest cover decreases, the removed area is redistributed between rainfed crops and grassland while maintaining their original proportions. If neither was present, it is divided equally between them.
When forest cover increases, the new forest proportionally replaces rainfed crops and grassland, up to the maximum area available across these two land-cover types.
Because forest has a higher evapotranspiration coefficient, reducing forest cover tends to decrease actual evapotranspiration and increase river contributions, while increasing it tends to have the opposite effect.






Note



A value of 100% retains the original cover; 50% halves it and 150% increases it by 50%, provided that sufficient rainfed crop and grassland area is available.

title: Creating and comparing scenarios
text:
Modifying a specific abstraction
For editable nodes, you can specify:

a total annual volume, which is distributed monthly;
different flow values for each month.

title: Creating and comparing scenarios
text:
Modifying reservoir releases
Reservoir releases can also be specified as:

an annual volume;
monthly values.

The model limits the release to the water actually available after accounting for inflow, storage and evaporation.

title: Getting started
text:
Your first simulation
When the application opens, it displays the reference scenario. For an initial exploration:

Select the simulation duration.
Keep the scenario’s initial values.
Press Apply.
Observe the colours of the river reaches and nodes.
Click a reach or node to view its information.
Switch between the period summary and a specific month.

title: Getting started
text:
Period summary and monthly view
The tool provides two main types of view:

Annual or multi-year summary
When viewing a summary for one or more years, the colours show how often an incident occurs, for example:

Number of months in which the environmental flow requirement is not met.
Number of months in which a demand cannot be met.

This view is useful for identifying persistent problems.


Specific month
When a month is selected, the legend becomes binary. Each element simply indicates whether, during that month, it:

Meets or fails to meet the environmental flow requirement.
Meets or fails to meet the demand.

This view is useful for studying specific seasonal situations.

title: Getting started
text:
Simple example
Try the following exercise:

Run the reference scenario.
Reduce precipitation by 20%.
Run the simulation again.
Compare:

reservoir inflow;
final stored volume;
reaches that fail to meet the environmental flow requirement;
unmet demands.








Tip



When interpreting a scenario, it is best to compare it with the reference scenario rather than analysing its values in isolation.

Reservoir balance
text:
The model represents the regulated Sau–Susqueda–Pasteral system in an aggregated manner.
For each month, storage is updated using a volume balance:
\[
V_{m+1}
=
V_m
+
Q^{in}_m S_m
-
Q^{rel}_m S_m
-
V^{evap}_m
-
V^{overflow}_m
\]
where:

\(V_m\): volume stored at the start of the month;
\(Q^{in}_m\): inflow;
\(Q^{rel}_m\): controlled release;
\(S_m\): duration of the month in seconds;
\(V^{evap}_m\): evaporation loss;
\(V^{overflow}_m\): overflow volume.

title: Reservoir balance
text:
Initial volume
The initial volume specified by the user is used in the first month. In subsequent months, the final volume from the previous month is used.

title: Reservoir balance
Reservoir balance
Reservoir balance
text:
User-defined release
The user can specify an annual volume or monthly values. The model always applies the physical constraint:
\[
V^{release}_m
\leq
V_m+V^{in}_m-V^{evap}_m
\]
Therefore, no more water can be released than is available.

title: Reservoir balance
text:
Overflow
When the resulting volume exceeds the maximum system capacity, the excess becomes overflow:
\[
V^{overflow}_m
=
\max(0,V^{provisional}_{m+1}-V^{max})
\]
The stored volume is limited to \(V^{max}\).

title: Flow routing and groundwater
text:
The model traverses the network in the direction of flow. At each node, it adds the flows arriving through upstream reaches and applies the corresponding local change.
The resulting flow is transferred to the downstream reaches.

Glossary
text:
Abstraction
Removal of water from the river for urban, agricultural or industrial use, or for a transfer.
Actual evapotranspiration (ET or AET)
The amount of water actually evaporated or transpired by vegetation according to climate and water availability.
Directed graph
A structure consisting of nodes and connections with a specific direction, in this case the direction of river flow.
Environmental flow
The minimum flow established to maintain the ecological functioning of the river.
Local contribution
Flow generated within a drainage area from the balance between precipitation, evapotranspiration and snow.
Node
A point in the network where flow is generated, modified, stored or assessed.
Overflow
Volume that exceeds the maximum storage capacity and leaves the system.
Potential evapotranspiration (PET)
The evaporative demand of the atmosphere if the available water were not limiting.
Reservoir storage
Volume of water held in the reservoirs.
Return
Water that returns to the river after use, such as effluent from a wastewater treatment plant.
River reach
A connection between two nodes through which flow is routed.
Scenario
A set of modifications applied to the reference conditions.
Unmet demand
The difference between the water requested and the water actually available at a node.
